To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the pollen record of the G6-4 marine core from the eastern Indian ocean provides a record of fire and vegetation change through the last three glacial cycles, and that the record suggests an anthropogenic influence on the landscape of eastern Australia from at least 200,000 BP.

Charcoal, elemental organic carbon (EOC), clastic particles and pollen have been analysed on core G6- 4 from the eastern Indian ocean to provide a detailed record of fire, vegetation and climate change over the last 300 000 years.
the record from G6-4 shows a record of fire, vegetation and climate change during the last three glacial cycles.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the reconstruction of the vegetation and climate of the Indonesian archipelago over the past 300,000 yr, and the relationship of these to the global climate record.
the nature and timing of changes in the vegetation and fire regimes of Lombok Ridge during the last glacial cycle and the possible role of humans in this process.
the development of the Australian biota and climate during the last 300 ka.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the record is a good proxy of the vegetation history of the region and that there is a strong possibility that the record is also a proxy of fire history, and that the record may be influenced by volcanic activity.
the pollen record is dominated by the effects of fire and that this has obscured a more detailed interpretation of the record of vegetation change and climatic change.
the record from G6-4 is consistent with a wetter interglacial and drier glacial regime in the region, with some evidence for anthropogenic burning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
fire, vegetation and climate have been closely linked over the last 300 ka in the region.

the last glacial–intergalcial cycles were associated with significant changes in fire regimes, vegetation disturbance and climate, and that these changes may well have been influenced by anthropogenic burning.

the Lombok Ridge is a valuable archive for reconstructing fire history and vegetation change in the region, but that the pollen record alone is insufficient to provide a clear picture of climate change.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need for more detailed and more frequent sampling of the core to better resolve the timing of the changes.
the pollen record from G6-4 is not an independent record of vegetation change and is best interpreted in the context of a changing climate and fire regime.

there is no evidence of a significant increase in burning or vegetation disturbance in the eastern Indian Ocean until about 200,00 years ago and that this is consistent with a relatively late arrival of humans into Australia.
